En 2020, la pandémie a mis en lumière un: In 2020, the pandemic brought to light a long-ignored reality in Montréal: menstrual insecurity.
En décembre dernier, Amina*, une lectric: Last December, Amina*, a La Converse reader, contacted us about a subject that hits close to home for her: menstrual insecurity. Having recently arrived in Canada, she was shocked by the cost of menstrual products. In her home country, Tunisia, a pack of sanitary pads costs only $2.
En discutant avec elle, nous l’avons ori: While talking with her, we pointed her to a few services in Montréal, including the subsidy program for buying menstrual products, which is run by the écoquartiers in each borough. But as I dug a little deeper, I realized that things weren’t as simple as they seemed. And when I talked about it with people around me, I discovered that many women don’t even know this service exists.
Pourquoi les Montréalaises sont-elles au: Why are Montréal women so poorly informed about this program? Thinking back, I realized that I, too, had never seen an ad or any communication about it.
Avec ce reportage, j’ai voulu non seulem: With this report, I wanted not only to shed light on what many women are going through, but also to find out what the boroughs are already doing. What budgets have been allocated? Is there significant demand? Why are some initiatives underused in certain neighbourhoods?
Pour cela, il m’a fallu m’armer de patie: To do this, I had to arm myself with patience and rigour. I contacted each of the boroughs to get answers to my questions. Some didn’t have the information I asked for, and others at first responded only partially. On top of that, as the holidays approached, communication became more and more difficult, which slowed down my efforts.
Cependant, ce travail de collecte d’info: Still, this work of gathering information made me realize how fragmented and little known access to these services is. This report doesn’t aim only to expose a problem, but also to offer ideas for improving how these services are communicated and how accessible this essential aid is.
Je tiens à remercier toutes celles et to: I would like to thank everyone who helped me dig into this subject, as well as Amina, who made this mini-investigation possible and allowed me to shed light on a reality that too often goes unrecognized.
<strong><em>En 2020, la pandémie a mis e: In 2020, the pandemic brought to light a long-ignored reality in Montréal: menstrual insecurity. To respond to it, initiatives such as the free distribution of disposable sanitary pads in public buildings were launched. The City also introduced subsidies for the purchase of reusable menstrual products, such as washable pads and reusable underwear, in 17 boroughs. Yet this program remains largely unknown, and the funds allocated are rarely used in full. At a time when the cost of menstrual products keeps rising, this initiative could be a solution. So why isn’t it reaching those who need it most? La Converse went to meet those directly affected. Report.
Vendredi 10 janvier. Sur le boulevard Sa: Friday, January 10. On Saint-Laurent Boulevard, the offices of the organization Collectif Bienvenue are tucked away on the 8th floor of a large building housing various businesses. Finding the way isn’t easy, but people coming to pick up mattresses guide us to the door of this community centre dedicated to emergency aid for asylum seekers.
À l’entrée, nous découvrons Selma, une i: At the entrance, we meet Selma, a worker with the organization. “We’re supposed to be closed to visitors today, but some people don’t know that. When they have urgent needs, I can’t really see myself telling them to come back next week,” she explains with a wry smile.
L’espace qu’occupe l’organisme, impeccab: The space the organization occupies, impeccably organized, almost feels like a warehouse: sections separated by large shelves are devoted to furniture, mattresses, armchairs, kitchen items and winter clothing. Among the imposing furniture, we find dozens of boxes filled with feminine hygiene products: tampons, thin and thick pads, and even reusable cups. “It’s true that women don’t expect to find menstrual products here. But when they find out, they’re surprised and relieved,” says Selma, pulling out a box. “We always put about ten pads in our kits for newcomers,” she continues. “If someone needs more, we give a whole pack. It’s not a problem for us, because we know it’s expensive… it’s very, very expensive,” she insists. “Some tell me, ‘Oh, I needed some, I had to buy them, but I couldn’t.’ Others say, ‘It’s expensive here, thank you. I was using cloth instead.’”
Chaque jour, au moins quatre paquets de: Every day, at least four packs of pads are handed out to a range of recipients: women in shelters, newcomers, and international students who don’t have a cent left in their accounts. “Honestly, we give them to anyone who might need them. For us, it’s like having toilet paper at home. You shouldn’t have to think about it.” And for these women, who are often in precarious situations, this simple gesture can make all the difference.
<strong>Des nouvelles arrivantes choquée: Newcomers shocked by the price of disposable sanitary pads
Cyrianne, 25 ans, est l’une des 200 béné: Cyrianne, 25, is one of the centre’s 200 volunteers. The young woman arrived alone from Guinea in January 2024. Self-conscious at the sight of the microphone, she smiles shyly and briefly describes her experience. “When I got my first kit with the sanitary pads, I was so happy and relieved!” she says, then continues: “In Guinea, a pack of 12 pads costs barely a dollar, but here, the price stopped me from buying any.”
Aujourd’hui encore, Cyrianne et les autr: Even today, Cyrianne and the other volunteers are allowed to take what they need from the menstrual product supplies. “The ones we have here are good quality; they smell nice,” she adds with a mischievous smile. “I know that if I couldn’t help myself here, I’d use toilet paper instead.” A volunteer with the community organization since April 2024, Cyrianne now makes sure that all those who might need pads get them when they come to the organization. Unfortunately, many people still don’t know that initiatives like this one exist.
C’est le cas d’Amina, 32 ans, arrivée au: That’s the case for Amina, 32, who arrived in Quebec as a skilled worker in July 2024. Confronted with menstrual insecurity for the first time after arriving on Turtle Island, she contacted La Converse so that we would shed light on this subject. To avoid any stigma, she preferred to speak with us by phone.
Arrivée sur le territoire québécois plei: She arrived in Quebec full of hope, began training programs with Services Québec and quickly bonded with other recently immigrated women. A burning topic soon emerged from their conversations: the cost of menstrual products.
« On était toutes d’accord pour dire que: “We all agreed that it was too expensive. In Tunisia, a pack of sanitary pads costs about 4 dinars, the equivalent of $2. Here, a pack costs between $8 and $15, and the quality isn’t even better,” she begins.
Ce constat, partagé par de nombreuses no: This observation, shared by many newcomers, turns an essential need into an unaffordable luxury. “Some women I’ve met have told me they avoid changing their pad too often, even if it causes them irritation. It’s a hard situation to live with,” she adds.
Avant son arrivée au Canada, Amina utili: Before arriving in Canada, Amina used a menstrual cup for environmental reasons. “Here, it’s become an economic choice,” she says. And adopting these new habits isn’t without constraints. “In my country, the toilets are equipped with bidets. It’s convenient for emptying and cleaning the cup. Here, in public washrooms, there’s no privacy, which complicates things a lot,” she explains.
Pour réduire les dépenses liées à l’acha: To cut the cost of buying sanitary pads, Amina keeps her menstrual cup in all day, for 12 hours – the maximum recommended – rather than changing it every 6 to 8 hours, as she used to. “I have to set priorities in my spending. I came with all my savings, but they’re not worth much here,” she says with resignation.
Depuis juillet 2015, les produits menstr: Since July 2015, menstrual products have no longer been taxed in Canada, a victory won thanks to the mobilization of the feminist collective Canadian Menstruators and its petition <l1>No Tax on Tampons</l1>. Although this measure is a step forward, it remains insufficient to meet the needs of women in precarious situations, says Amina: “It’s true that they’re tax-free, but the prices of menstrual products just keep going up, so financially we don’t feel the tax break.”
Les données de Statistique Canada révèle: Data from Statistics Canada does show a 3% increase in the price of menstrual products from June 2023 to June 2024. This adds to a general increase of more than 10% in the price of personal care products over the past two years. And as early as 2019, the Canadian Public Health Association estimated that a woman spent about $6,000 on disposable menstrual products over her lifetime.
Face à cette augmentation, des organisme: Faced with this increase, organizations such as Dignité Mensuelle, a supplier of menstrual products to Collectif Bienvenue, are working to offer concrete solutions and to raise public awareness of the urgent need to act against menstrual insecurity.
« La précarité menstruelle peut toucher: “Menstrual insecurity can affect anyone, at different points in life,” says Estelle Beauclair, educational programs coordinator at the organization Dignité Mensuelle. The young woman points to the silence surrounding the phenomenon: “We often associate this insecurity with people living in deep poverty, but it also affects single mothers who put their children’s needs before their own, newcomers who are struggling to make ends meet, and low-income students.”
Certaines personnes comme celles en situ: Some people, such as people with disabilities, queer people and students, are even more vulnerable because of their social or economic situation, she explains.
Revenant sur ses années universitaires,: Looking back on her university years, Estelle tells us: “I would buy a few menstrual products, then use toilet paper. At the time, it didn’t seem that serious. I preferred being able to keep a roof over my head.” With hindsight, she now recognizes that this situation, which was treated as normal at the time, was menstrual insecurity.
« Et les conséquences de cette précarité: “And the consequences of this insecurity go well beyond discomfort,” she insists. “It’s not uncommon to hear people say they wear the same pad for 24 hours, layer panty liners – which are cheaper – or use newspaper, or even socks,” she laments.
<strong>Une personne menstruée sur cinq: One in five people who menstruate in Quebec has used alternatives (toilet paper, cloth, etc.) in place of menstrual products because of their price. Source: Portrait du vécu des menstruations au Québec, RQASF
Ces pratiques augmentent les risques d’i: These practices increase the risk of serious infections, notably toxic shock syndrome, which can lead to severe complications such as amputations or even death, warns <l1>OXFAM France.</l1>
Selon Estelle, la précarité menstruelle: According to Estelle, menstrual insecurity is not attributable only to financial hardship. It is also amplified by limited access to safe facilities and suitable products.
Certaines femmes sont davantage exposées: Some women are more exposed to this reality. “A woman experiencing homelessness who suffers from endometriosis might need specific products, thicker and longer-lasting. But those items are often not accessible to her,” Estelle explains. The lack of regular access to safe washrooms also exposes these people to increased health risks. Their precarious situation also keeps them away from medical care, a situation made worse by the lack of an address, the lack of a family doctor and the prejudice they face, she continues.
<strong>Les conditions de la sécurité me: The conditions for menstrual security, according to Dignité Mensuelle
<strong>Accès à des produits menstruels: Access to suitable menstrual products: offering solutions that match individual needs.
<strong>Accès à des salles de bain sécur: Access to safe washrooms: open 24 hours a day, with doors that close properly.
<strong>Accès à l’eau courante :</strong: Access to running water: facilities for washing hands and for cleaning reusable menstrual products.
<strong>Accès à des soins médicaux :</st: Access to medical care: to treat menstrual illnesses or disorders, such as endometriosis and polycystic ovary syndrome, and to support menopausal women.‍
<strong>Accès à des poubelles :</strong>: Access to garbage bins: to dispose of menstrual products hygienically and discreetly.
En 2024, 55 organismes ont reçu des prod: In 2024, 55 organizations received menstrual hygiene products supplied by Dignité Mensuelle, Estelle reports. “Most of the time, these are regular donations. We try to make a delivery every six to eight weeks,” she says.
Pour y parvenir, l’équipe loue deux véhi: To manage this, the team rents two vehicles and divides up routes across different areas of the city. “On our last delivery, in mid-December, we served eight or nine organizations”, she adds proudly.
Cependant, face à la pression croissante: However, faced with mounting pressure, the organization sometimes has to redirect requests it can’t fulfill to municipal services. “The needs are immense. Sometimes we’re talking about 5,000 tampons a month… We can’t meet every request,” says the young woman, visibly disappointed.
En 2021, la Ville de Montréal a mis en p: In 2021, the City of Montréal launched <l1>a pilot project offering free disposable menstrual products in several municipal buildings</l1>. The products were initially available at City Hall, the Montréal Botanical Garden, the Ahuntsic library and the Jean-Claude-Malépart community centre. This well-received initiative has been expanded to other locations over time. However, it isn’t without flaws.
« On nous rapporte souvent des ruptures: “We often hear reports of stock shortages. The products are sometimes unavailable, or people have to ask for them explicitly,” Estelle laments. On top of that, the selection of products remains limited. “Sometimes only tampons are available, which is neither inclusive nor entirely safe for everyone. That said, the initiative is a good one, but adjustments are needed.”
Depuis 2020, la Ville de Montréal dispos: Since 2020, the City of Montréal has had <l1>a subsidy program for the purchase of reusable menstrual products</l1>, run by the écoquartiers in each borough. People who have bought washable pads, menstrual cups or reusable period underwear can request partial reimbursement, under the conditions of the borough where the request is submitted.
Cependant, une enquête menée en 2023 par: However, a 2023 survey by the Réseau québécois d’action pour la santé des femmes (RQASF) highlighted some significant gaps: nearly half of respondents did not know that subsidies for buying reusable menstrual products existed in their neighbourhood.
Élise Brunot, directrice du RQASF, conna: Élise Brunot, director of the RQASF, knows this subject particularly well, having worked on it before.
« On voit qu’il y a des arrondissements: “We see that there are boroughs where the subsidies run out extremely quickly, while others struggle to get rid of them,” she notes. This situation is attributable in part to budget gaps between boroughs and differences in how funds are allocated.
Les disparités budgétaires sont en effet: The budget disparities are indeed striking. Mercier–Hochelaga-Maisonneuve, which had a budget of $57,500, used only 35% of the funds allocated, and Saint-Léonard, with a modest envelope of $2,500, had a usage rate of barely 16%. By contrast, boroughs such as Ahuntsic-Cartierville, Ville-Marie and Le Plateau-Mont-Royal handed out all of their subsidies.
Selon Élise, ces écarts s’expliquent en: According to Élise, these gaps are partly explained by the approaches taken: “Some boroughs fold these subsidies into other programs, like the one for washable diapers. Depending on the approach, it makes a big difference. An envelope dedicated solely to reusable menstrual products would have more impact.”
À ces disparités, Élise ajoute le manque: To these disparities, Élise adds the lack of awareness in certain areas. “It’s obvious that on the Plateau, it reaches its target more easily than in boroughs like Montréal-Nord or Hochelaga,” she begins. “The audience is different: they don’t necessarily have the same access to this kind of subject or the same awareness of how useful reusable menstrual products are.”
Malgré les efforts de sensibilisation de: Despite her organization’s awareness efforts, Élise acknowledges that it remains hard to reach everyone affected, especially those who need it most. “I’m going to draw a caricature that seems pretty realistic to me, but when you don’t have much money, when you’re a single mother, you don’t necessarily want to bother with underwear and pads that you have to soak and wash. You go for the simplest, most effective option: disposable – even if it’s more expensive in the long run.”

Autre frein majeur : la communication. S: Another major obstacle: communication. According to Élise, not all boroughs promote these programs clearly. “You get tired of asking for the reimbursement, so in the end, you give up. Some of the steps are a real obstacle course. Sometimes you have to go to the borough office with a receipt; other times, everything is done online, and you have to scan your receipt if it isn’t a digital one. So that inevitably excludes everyone who doesn’t have the necessary tools or skills.”
Elle ajoute : « Les sites Web de certain: She adds: “Some boroughs’ websites aren’t user-friendly; they’re old. Personally, I submitted a request, but I never got any response, not even an acknowledgment of receipt. Still, I got a reimbursement after three months.”

« Les produits menstruels durables, ça c: “Reusable menstrual products cost a fortune,” continues the woman, who recently restocked her period underwear. “I spent a little over $250, but I only got a $50 reimbursement, which isn’t great either. In the long run, it’s obviously cheaper than buying disposable pads. But right now, it’s an extremely high upfront cost. That $200, you have to come up with it.”
<strong>Trois personnes sur 10 souhaiter: Three in 10 people would like to use reusable products but find them too expensive. Source: Portrait du vécu des menstruations au Québec, RQASF
Quant aux alternatives, comme la coupe,: As for alternatives like the cup, Élise sees it as a less costly solution, but not without constraints: “You have to be able to go to a washroom where you have a sink available. In the stall, not outside.”
De plus, le taux de remboursement varie: In addition, the reimbursement rate also varies from one borough to another: some cover up to 75% of the costs, others 50%, and still others offer more modest amounts, with a maximum reimbursement of $50.
Pour Élise, il est évident que le progra: For Élise, it’s clear that the subsidy program would gain in popularity and accessibility if it were run by the City rather than by the écoquartiers. “There would be fewer disparities in reimbursements,” she begins. “There would be stronger communication, there would be consistency in how things are done, in the forms, and so on. It could also be done in a hybrid way – online, but also in person, at a meeting point to make things easier.”
Contactée à ce sujet, la Ville de Montré: Contacted about this, the City of Montréal had not responded to our questions at the time of writing.
Malgré tout, Élise reste optimiste : « Ç: Despite everything, Élise remains optimistic: “It’s moving slowly, but surely. I’m hopeful that over time it will become widespread and run more smoothly. In 2020, when we started these campaigns, nobody was talking about it. In 2025, you have to admit that the progress made is impressive.”
Pour Élise, les défis liés au coût, à l’: For Élise, the challenges tied to cost, accessibility and even subsidies reveal a broader problem: that of raising awareness among everyone. “Education is at the heart of all this,” she insists. “If, from a young age, we taught young people about menstruation, how to manage it and the alternatives available, we would reduce a lot of inequalities.”
Elle plaide pour une approche proactive: She advocates for a proactive approach that would include distributing menstrual products in schools and broader access to information. “It starts with eliminating taboos and building this education into institutions.”
